nameStory: Black cherry gets its name from its dark, nearly black fruits that ripen in late summer. The species name 'serotina' comes from Latin meaning 'late,' referring to how it blooms later than most other cherries in spring. It's also called rum cherry because early colonists used the fruit to flavor alcoholic beverages.
description: Black cherry is a medium to large deciduous tree that can grow 50-80 feet tall with a straight trunk and oval crown. It's a member of the rose family, despite not being closely related to the sweet cherries we eat. The tree produces drooping clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by small dark cherries that birds love. Its distinctive dark, scaly bark makes it easy to spot year-round.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to nearly black bark that breaks into distinctive potato chip-like scales or plates, especially on older trees. Run your hand along it - it feels rough and scaly, quite different from the smooth bark of younger trees.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Long, drooping clusters (4-6 inches) of small white flowers appear in late spring after leaves emerge. Each tiny flower has 5 white petals and gives off a faint, sweet fragrance that attracts bees and flies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Alternate, oval leaves 2-5 inches long with finely serrated edges that feel slightly rough. Look for tiny orange or red glands along the leaf stem near the base - a key identifying feature you can feel with your fingertip.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small round cherries, about pea-sized, that ripen from red to dark purple or black in late summer. They taste astringent and bitter, quite different from sweet cultivated cherries, with a large pit inside.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a straight, tall tree with a narrow oval crown when mature. Young trees have smoother, reddish-brown bark with horizontal lines called lenticels that look like dashes.

habitat: Black cherry thrives throughout New England in well-drained soils, from rich bottomlands to dry hillsides and forest edges. You'll find it in mixed hardwood forests alongside maples, oaks, and hickories, as well as in old fields growing back to forest. It's quite adaptable and grows from sea level to mountain slopes up to 2,000 feet elevation.

seasonality.spring: Long drooping clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in May after leaves have emerged, later than most other cherries. New leaves unfold with a bronze-green tint and those distinctive glands along the leaf stems.
seasonality.summer: Full green foliage provides dense shade, and small cherries ripen from green to red to dark purple-black by late summer. This is when the fruit-eating birds have their feast.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange before dropping, and you might still find some dried cherries clinging to branches. The distinctive scaly bark becomes more prominent as a winter identification feature.
seasonality.winter: The dark, scaly bark and straight trunk make identification easy. Reddish-brown buds are small and pointed, and you might spot old flower clusters still attached to twigs.

funFact: Black cherry wood is one of America's most prized cabinet woods, so valuable that large trees were historically called 'cherry gold' - a single mature tree can be worth thousands of dollars to furniture makers for its beautiful reddish heartwood that deepens with age.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with chokecherry, but black cherry grows much larger (chokecherry stays shrub-sized) and has the distinctive scaly bark. Remember: 'Black cherry, scaly bark' - chokecherry has smooth, grayish bark with horizontal lines.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cherry,' black cherry isn't closely related to the sweet or sour cherries we eat, which come from different Prunus species. The leaves and bark contain compounds that can be toxic to livestock, especially when wilted, so farmers often remove these trees from pastures.
compareHints: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark. Chokecherry stays shrub-sized with smooth bark, while fire cherry (pin cherry) is smaller with reddish, peeling bark. Black cherry also blooms later than its relatives and has longer flower clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
